title: B-R-A
hook: bara: to create, in the Torah used only of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, M-Ch-L: mechilah, waiving what you're owed. Your line was let it go. Did you put one piece of paper down before you slept? Today, a new week, and the verb in the Torah's opening line. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

The Torah's opening line has a subject and a verb in it. The subject is God. The verb is bara. Bereshit bara Elohim. In the beginning, God created. English is generous with create. People create playlists, create problems, create a stir at the dinner table. Hebrew has plenty of words for making and building, and people use those all the time. But this one, in the Torah, is kept to a single subject. Today's root is three letters: bet, resh, alef. B-R-A. A verb with a reserved seat.
screen: `BERESHIT BARA ELOHIM.` → `CREATE A PLAYLIST?` → `B-R-A: A RESERVED VERB.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the subject. Jewish commentators point out that in the Torah, bara is used only of God. People make, build, shape and plant. God creates. The verb itself becomes a quiet statement about who is doing what. Second, the surprises. In the first chapter of Genesis, bara turns up at the very start, "God created the heaven and the earth," and then it goes quiet. When it returns, it's for something unexpected: "And God created the great sea-monsters." Not the sun, not the trees, but the creatures of the deep. Some readers take that as a hint that even the things people fear most are inside creation, not outside it. Then it comes again, three times in one verse, for human beings. Third, the pair. When the creation story ends, on the seventh day, the text uses two verbs side by side. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, God rested from all His work "which God in creating had made." Creating, bara. Made, asah. Some Jewish commentators linger on the Hebrew there, which can be read as created to make, and hear in it an unfinished world: God creates, and leaves the making to go on, in human hands. Fourth, the heart. A psalm asks for this verb to happen again, inside a person: "Create me a clean heart, O God." Not fix, not repair. Create. As if some things need more than patching. So the verb sits at the top of the Torah and returns in a prayer, as a request for something new.
screen: `THE SUBJECT: ONLY GOD CREATES.` · `THE SURPRISE: THE GREAT SEA-MONSTERS.` · `THE PAIR: CREATED, AND MADE.` · `THE HEART: CREATE ME A CLEAN HEART.` · then, large: `בָּרָא`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: create something small. Not something useful, not something anyone will grade. Settle, and breathe. Then, while the bell holds the time, make one small thing that wasn't here a minute ago. A line of words. A doodle in a margin. A few notes hummed in an order you've never hummed them. A paper fold. Don't fix it, don't judge it. Just notice what it's like to bring one new thing into the room. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's line about a clean heart while you work. The bell holds the time.
B-R-A. Bet, resh, alef: the root of bara, to create, the verb of the Torah's opening line, which in the Torah has God as its subject. Today's word.

Your line: create. Today, keep the small thing you made somewhere you'll see it, and let it remind you of the commentators who read the world as left with making still to do. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Jews begin the yearly cycle of Torah reading with Bereshit, "in the beginning," and Jewish commentators often note that the verb bara, to create, is reserved in the Torah for God.
